items.title: Four particles, four jobs

cells.note: This particle never takes a preverbal pronoun.
Its clause always depends on another clause.

items.caption: Mood particles fill the tense particle’s slot but say how the event is wanted, waited for or warned against, rather than when it happens.

items.title: Purpose with or without a joining word

states.label: With *ʻina*
states.sm: Tatalo ʻina ʻia maua se fesoasoani.
states.en: Pray in order to get some help.
states.note: The joining word explicitly marks the purpose clause as part of the first sentence.

states.label: Without *ʻina*
states.note: The second clause still expresses purpose, even though no joining word shows the link.

items.caption: Both printed sentences express what the praying is for. The first one marks the link with *ʻina*.

items.title: Read the mood in its clause

data.question: What is the particle doing in this sentence?

prompts.why: About the speaker, *seʻi* politely asks permission.
Addressed to the listener, *ʻia* makes a polite command.
The waiting lasts until the event after *seʻia*.

prompts.sm: Tatalo ʻina ʻia maua se fesoasoani.
prompts.why: The linked *ʻia* clause says what the praying is for.

items.intro: Use the whole sentence to identify the job of the mood clause.

items.title: The pronoun changes sides

states.label: With *te*
states.note: The preverbal pronoun stands before the general particle’s *te* form.

states.label: With *neʻi*
states.note: The pronoun stands behind the warning particle.

items.caption: Both printed forms forbid dancing. The pronoun comes before *te* and after *neʻi*, so changing the particle changes their order.

items.title: Let me, let us, or may it happen
items.intro: Read the English, then choose the Sāmoan sentence that says it.

prompts.why: *ʻIa* asks plainly for what is wanted, and *tātou* is we, you and I. With *ʻe* the same request is made to the listener alone: be patient.
*Seʻi* about the speaker, with *oʻu* for I, asks permission. *Seʻi sau le tama* is about someone else, so it is a wish.
*Seʻi* about someone who is neither the speaker nor the listener says the speaker wants it to happen. *Seʻia* means until: wait until the boy comes.
*Seʻi oʻu* puts the speaker in the clause, so it politely asks permission. *Seʻi sau se isi* wishes for someone else to come.
